items.title: Grocery Prices Sit 22% Above 2021 Levels as Near-Record Diesel Raises Costs From Farm to Store
items.excerpt: September price data show food at home costs 22.5% more than five years ago, while diesel above $6 a gallon adds pressure that has not fully reached store shelves. ... Americans are paying about 22% more for groceries than they did five years ago, and the latest federal price data arrived as diesel — the fuel that powers tractors, freight trucks and refrigerated trailers — holds near its record high. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' food-at-home index stood at 321.758 in September 2026, compared with 262.695 in September 2021, a 22.5% increase, according to BLS figures compiled by the St. Louis Fed. The monthly picture looks calmer. Grocery prices slipped 0.1% in September and were 1.8% higher than a year earlier, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in its latest Consumer Price Index release. But a slower annual rate does not erase five years of accumulated increases, and several of the foods most closely tied to a balanced diet are still rising faster than the grocery average. Fuel is what makes the next few months hard to call. The national average price of diesel was $6.33 a gallon on Oct. 16, up 68% from $3.76 before the U.S.-Iran war began, according to AAA figures cited by the Associated Press. Diesel hit a record $6.53 in September. No federal agency has yet measured how much of that cost will reach retail food prices, and economists quoted by the AP said much of it has not shown up so far. ... The September report shows a split grocery aisle. Fresh fruits were up 4.9% from a year earlier, fruits and vegetables overall rose 3.7%, coffee climbed 7.1%, and beef rose 3.5%, according to the BLS detailed tables. Eggs fell 20.6%, and dairy dipped 0.7%, which helped hold the overall grocery figure down. ... Eating out remains the bigger budget strain. Prices for food away from home rose 3.5% over the year, nearly double the grocery rate. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service now forecasts grocery prices will rise 2.4% in 2026, with fresh vegetables up 5.7% and beef and veal up 9.4%, while eggs are expected to fall 29.4%. The AP reported that USDA's forecast before the war called for a 1.7% grocery increase this year. ... The fuel effect starts on the farm. A Farm Bureau analysis by Deputy Chief Economist Faith Parum and Associate Economist Cameron Castillo found farm diesel in Illinois, as reported by USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service, rose from $3.01 a gallon in September 2025 to $5.61 in September 2026. The American Farm Bureau Federation is a farm advocacy organization, and its estimates rely on representative farm models rather than surveys of actual bills. ... Freight data point the same way. September producer-price data showed truck freight prices up 19.3% from a year earlier, while transportation and warehousing of goods sold to businesses cost 10.2% more, the AP reported. Those indexes track what carriers charge, not what shoppers pay. USDA also raised its 2026 estimates of fuel, lubricant and electricity costs for major crops by 33% to 41%, according to the AP. ... The evidence has limits, and they matter. The 22% five-year figure is a measured price index, but the share of today's prices caused by diesel is not. The AP noted it is unclear how much of this year's increase stems from the war versus tariffs, weather, or labor costs. Experts have warned that fresh produce and other frequently restocked perishables could respond fastest to higher transportation and refrigeration costs, so those are the categories to watch.

items.title: US inflation rose slightly last month after 2 years of steady cooling but remained low
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — Inflation in the United States ticked up in October, driven by costlier rents, used cars and air fares, a sign that price increases might be leveling off after having slowed in September to their lowest pace since 2021. Consumer prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 2.4% in September. It was the first rise in annual inflation in seven months. From September to October, prices edged up 0.2%, the same as the previous month. Excluding volatile food and energy costs, “core” prices rose 3.3% from a year earlier, the same as in September. From September to October, core prices rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Over the long run, core inflation at that pace would exceed the Fed’s 2% target. ... An uptick in prices, if sustained, could stir concerns in financial markets that progress in taming inflation may be slowing. It might also make the Federal Reserve less inclined to cut its key interest rate in the coming months, as its officials have previously indicated they likely would. ... Still, most economists think inflation will eventually resume its slowdown. Consumer inflation, which peaked at 9.1% in 2022, has since fallen steadily, though overall prices are still about 20% higher than they were three years ago. ... At a news conference last week, Fed Chair Jerome Powell expressed confidence that inflation is still heading down to the central bank’s 2% target, though perhaps slowly and unevenly. Powell also noted that most sources of price pressures are cooling, suggesting that inflation isn’t likely to accelerate in the coming months. Wages are still growing and have outpaced prices for the past year and a half. But Powell noted that wages aren’t rising quickly enough to boost inflation. ... A survey released Tuesday by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that consumers expect prices to rise just 2.9% in the next 12 months, which would be the lowest such measure in nearly four years. Lower inflation expectations are important because when consumers expect milder price increases, they’re less likely to act in ways that raise inflation, such as accelerating their purchases or demanding higher pay to offset higher prices. ... Another potential source of relief for Americans’ budgets is in apartment rents. They are now barely rising on average nationwide, according to the real estate brokerage Redfin. Its measure of median rent was just 0.2% higher than it was a year ago in October, at $1,619, though that figure reflects rents only for new leases.

items.title: U.S. Premiere of LAIKA's 'Wildwood' to Open 40th AFI FEST | Animation World Network
items.excerpt: LAIKA has set the U.S. premiere of its highly-anticipated new film, Wildwood, at the 40th edition of AFI FEST presented by Canva on Wednesday, October 21, at the TCL Chinese Theatres in Hollywood, two days before the epic stop-motion fantasy hits theaters nationwide through Fathom Entertainment. The film is a long time coming: Travis Knight directs and produces from a screenplay by Chris Butler, based on the novel by Colin Meloy, which LAIKA optioned way back in 2011. Caleb Deschanel handles cinematography; Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay lead the voice cast, alongside Carey Mulligan, Academy Award winner Mahershala Ali, Angela Bassett, Awkwafina, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Amandla Stenberg, Jemaine Clement, Maya Erskine, Tantoo Cardinal, Tom Waits and Richard E. Grant. In the film, after her baby brother is abducted by a murder of crows, headstrong teenager Prue McKeel (Lee) launches a desperate rescue mission into the Impassable Wilderness, an enchanted forest hidden just beyond Portland, Oregon. Joined by her hapless but loyal classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Tremblay), Prue navigates a world of talking animals, bandits and powerful figures driven by grief and ambition. As the pair is drawn into a conflict threatening the balance of the forest itself, Prue must discover the strength and belief she never knew she possessed. ... AFI FEST runs October 21-25 at the TCL Chinese Theatres, with Red Carpet Premieres, Special Screenings, World Cinema, Documentaries and Short Films. The full lineup will be unveiled September 29, individual tickets go on sale October 3, and passes are available now at FEST.AFI.com. The festival is an Academy Awards qualifying festival for the Live Action, Animated and Documentary Short Film categories.
